summary: The EU AI Act is the world's first comprehensive legal framework for artificial intelligence, establishing a risk-based approach to AI regulation across the European Union. It classifies AI systems into four risk tiers and imposes obligations proportional to the level of risk posed.

risk_tiers.description: AI systems that pose a clear threat to safety, livelihoods, or fundamental rights of persons. These systems are prohibited from being placed on the market or put into service in the EU.
criteria: Social scoring by public authorities leading to detrimental treatment
Real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement (with limited exceptions)
Exploitation of vulnerabilities of specific groups (age, disability, social situation)
Subliminal manipulation techniques causing physical or psychological harm
Emotion recognition in workplace and educational institutions
Untargeted scraping of facial images from internet or CCTV for facial recognition databases

risk_tiers.description: AI systems that pose significant risks to health, safety, or fundamental rights. Subject to strict requirements including conformity assessments, risk management, and human oversight before market placement.
criteria: Biometric identification and categorisation of natural persons
Management and operation of critical infrastructure (energy, transport, water)
Education and vocational training (determining access or assessing students)
Employment, worker management, and access to self-employment (recruitment, promotion, termination decisions)
Access to essential private and public services (credit scoring, insurance pricing)
Law enforcement (individual risk assessments, polygraphs, evidence evaluation)
Migration, asylum, and border control management
Administration of justice and democratic processes

risk_tiers.description: AI systems with specific transparency obligations. Users must be informed they are interacting with an AI system, and certain content must be labeled as AI-generated.
criteria: AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons (chatbots)
AI systems generating synthetic audio, image, video, or text content (deepfakes)
Emotion recognition systems (outside prohibited contexts)
Biometric categorisation systems (outside high-risk contexts)

risk_tiers.description: AI systems posing minimal or no risk to rights or safety. No mandatory requirements beyond existing legislation, though voluntary codes of conduct are encouraged.
criteria: AI-enabled video games
Spam filters
Inventory management systems
AI systems not falling into higher risk categories

key_obligations.obligation: Establish and maintain a risk management system throughout the AI system lifecycle, including identification, analysis, and mitigation of known and foreseeable risks
Implement data governance practices ensuring training, validation, and testing datasets are relevant, representative, free of errors, and complete
Draw up technical documentation demonstrating compliance before the system is placed on the market or put into service
Design AI systems to enable automatic recording of events (logs) for traceability throughout the system lifecycle
Ensure transparency and provision of information to deployers, including clear instructions for use, intended purpose, and known limitations
Design high-risk AI systems to allow effective human oversight, including the ability to understand, monitor, and override the system
Achieve appropriate levels of accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity throughout the system lifecycle
Inform natural persons that they are interacting with an AI system unless obvious from the circumstances

enforcement_timeline: Entered into force August 1, 2024. Prohibited practices apply from February 2, 2025. High-risk obligations apply from August 2, 2026. Full application by August 2, 2027.
recent_changes: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 published in Official Journal on July 12, 2024
AI Office established within the European Commission to oversee implementation
General-purpose AI model provisions added covering foundation models and systemic risk
